claims.text: Stripe reported that over 1,300 pull requests merged each week are completely minion-produced, up from 1,000 as of Part 1; they are human-reviewed but contain no human-written code.
Stripe's Part 1 post (dated 2026-02-09) reported over a thousand pull requests merged each week that are completely minion-produced, human-reviewed, and contain no human-written code.
InfoQ's 2026-03-20 report said Stripe's Minions produce over 1,300 pull requests per week, up from 1,000 in earlier trials.
A Stripe devbox is an AWS EC2 instance that contains Stripe's source code and runs services under development; Minions run on the same standard developer environment that Stripe engineers use.
Stripe aims for a devbox to be ready within 10 seconds by proactively provisioning and warming a pool of devboxes.

Devbox warm-up includes cloning large git repositories, warming Bazel and type-checking caches, and starting code generation services; a ready box has a recent copy of master across Stripe's main repos.
Devboxes are 'cattle, not pets': standardized and easy to replace, and many engineers use one devbox per task, sometimes about half a dozen at once.
Stripe's devboxes run in its QA environment, so Minions have no access to real user data, Stripe's production services, or arbitrary network egress.
Because mistakes are confined to the limited blast radius of one devbox, Stripe runs Minions with full permissions and no confirmation prompts.
Stripe has an internal security control framework to ensure Minions cannot use their MCP tools to perform destructive actions.

Blueprints are workflows defined in code that direct a Minion run; each node runs either deterministic code or an agent loop, so the Minion blueprint resembles a state machine mixing deterministic and free-flowing agent nodes.
The Minion blueprint's agent nodes include 'Implement task' and 'Fix CI failures', while deterministic nodes such as 'Run configured linters' and 'Push changes' invoke no LLM and just run code.
Stripe says deterministic code for predictable steps, such as always linting at the end of a run, saves tokens and CI costs at scale and gives the agent less opportunity to get things wrong.
Stripe has over three million tests, which provide feedback to Minions; it is infeasible to run all of them locally, so the standard blueprint includes one iteration against the full CI suite.
A local executable uses heuristics to select and automatically run lints on each git push, taking less than five seconds.
After a Minion pushes, CI runs and auto-applies autofixes for failing tests; failures with no autofix go back to a blueprint agent node for one more local fix attempt.
Stripe limits Minions to at most two rounds of CI; after the second push and CI run, the branch is sent back to its human operator for manual scrutiny.
Stripe limits CI rounds because CI runs cost tokens, compute and time, and it sees diminishing marginal returns from indefinitely many full CI loops.
A typical Minion run starts in a Slack message and ends in a pull request that passes CI and is ready for human review, with no interaction in between.

A Minion creates a branch, pushes it to CI, and prepares a pull request following Stripe's PR template; the engineer then requests review from another Stripe engineer, or gives the Minion further instructions.
Stripe forked Block's coding agent goose in late 2024 and customized it to work within Stripe's LLM infrastructure.

Minions use MCP via Toolshed, Stripe's central internal MCP server hosting more than 400 tools, to gather internal documentation, ticket details, build statuses and Sourcegraph code intelligence; agents get curated subsets.
Engineers noted Minions perform best on well-defined tasks such as configuration adjustments, dependency upgrades, and minor refactoring.
Stripe notes that in a large codebase an agent without guidance may struggle to follow best practices or use the proper libraries even with good linters.
The code Minions work on supports more than $1 trillion in annual payment volume at Stripe, with a backend mostly in Ruby (not Rails) with Sorbet typing.
